h1: Pollution control board consent for a brewery in India
title: Pollution Control Consent for a Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: What pollution control board consent means for a brewery in India: consent to establish and operate, wastewater, emissions, waste and how to prepare.
teaser: The brewhouse is installed and the excise inspector is happy. The pollution control board has not been asked yet.
standfirst: Every brewery produces wastewater, solid waste and usually some emissions. In India, that brings the state pollution control board into your project. Here is what consent involves and why to start early.
sections:
Brewing uses a lot of water and sends much of it back out, carrying sugars, yeast, proteins and cleaning chemicals. That effluent has high organic load, measured as biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD), far above domestic sewage. Breweries also produce spent grain, spent yeast and trub. A boiler or diesel generator adds air emissions.

Under India's water and air pollution laws, industries that discharge effluent or emissions need consent from the state pollution control board, or the pollution control committee in union territories. Breweries have generally been placed in the stricter categories for this, though some states treat small brewpubs differently. Check with your state board.
Consent to establish, then consent to operate

Consent usually comes in two stages:

  1. Consent to establish (CTE). Obtained before construction, based on your planned process, capacity, water use, effluent treatment and emissions.
  2. Consent to operate (CTO). Obtained before production, once the board is satisfied your treatment and controls are in place. It is renewed periodically.

Many excise departments and banks ask for pollution consent before they move forward. Apply early. Starting the process after the brewhouse is installed is a common and costly delay.

Expect the board to look closely at effluent. That usually means an effluent treatment plant (ETP) designed for brewery wastewater, or a connection to a common treatment facility where allowed, plus discharge standards for the treated water. Board conditions may cover parameters such as pH, BOD, COD and suspended solids, along with how often you test and report.

Cleaning-in-place cycles swing effluent pH sharply, from caustic washes to acid rinses. A balancing tank that evens out those swings before treatment saves a lot of trouble downstream. Sizing the ETP well needs a realistic estimate of water use per litre of beer, which depends heavily on how carefully the brewery cleans and rinses. Our sustainability in brewing guide covers how to bring that ratio down.

Spent grain is the largest solid by-product. In India it often goes to dairy farmers as cattle feed. Spent yeast and hop residue need planned disposal too. Boards may ask how each waste stream is handled, by whom and how often. Keep records of who collects what. Our guide to brewery waste and spent grain explains the options.

Used oil from generators and some chemical containers may fall under hazardous waste rules, with their own authorisation and disposal requirements.

Boilers and diesel generators need stacks of the right height and emissions within limits. They may need their own consent conditions. Refrigeration plants and compressors add noise that the board and neighbours may care about. If you choose an electric or gas-fired steam system rather than diesel, explain that in your application.
Water use is where savings start

The less water you use per litre of beer, the smaller your effluent volume, the smaller your ETP and the lower your treatment costs. Simple measures help: meter water at the brewhouse, cellar and packaging separately, recover hot water from wort cooling for the next brew or for cleaning, fix leaking hoses and use spray balls and CIP cycles that are timed rather than left running. Our guide to brewery utilities covers metering in more detail.

A brewery that can show the board measured water use and a plan to cut it makes a stronger application than one that guesses.

Rules vary by state and change, so check the current procedure on your state board's portal. Applications typically need:

  • A process description and production capacity.
  • Water source and estimated water consumption.
  • Effluent quantity, characteristics and treatment design.
  • Solid waste and emissions details.
  • Site plans and supporting approvals.

Many founders use an environmental consultant to prepare the application and design the ETP. It is money well spent if it avoids a rejection or a redesign.
Compliance does not stop at consent

Once you have consent, you must run within its conditions: operate the ETP properly, test effluent, keep records and renew on time. An ETP that is switched off to save power is a real risk to the licence. Treat it like any other piece of brewery kit, with a named owner, a maintenance schedule and logs.

Environmental compliance is increasingly part of how investors, banks and customers judge breweries. Getting it right from the start is cheaper than fixing it later.
faqs: Does a brewpub need pollution control board consent?
In most states, yes, because brewing produces effluent and waste. Some states treat small brewpubs differently, so check with your state board.
What is the difference between CTE and CTO?
Consent to establish is obtained before construction. Consent to operate is obtained before production starts and is renewed periodically.
Do I need an effluent treatment plant?
Usually, unless you can connect to an approved common facility. The board sets discharge standards for treated water.
